title: The arrow already flying
hookLine: an arrow is already flying when the archer sees the tiger was a cow
carry: prarabdha: old arrows land, no new ones drawn

lines: A STRIPED SHAPE IN THE GRASS.
WHY DOES THE FREE ONE STILL CATCH COLDS?
cards: An archer at the edge of a field sees a striped shape in the long grass. A tiger. He lets the arrow go, and in the half second after it leaves the string, the shape lifts its head.
It's a cow. He knows the truth now, completely. But the arrow is already in the air, and knowing can't call it back.
The Vivekachudamani tells this little story late in the book to answer a hard question. If knowing sets someone free, why does the free person still have a body, still get hungry, still catch a cold?

teach.b: Its answer, in paraphrase: actions set in motion before knowing dawns are like that arrow. Their name is prarabdha, the karma that has already begun.
Knowing doesn't stop them; they play out, and the body that came with them lives on until they're spent.
What knowing stops is the next arrow. The one who sees clearly no longer draws the bow from fear, from grabbing, from the old mistake about who they are.
The book calls such a person jivanmukta, free while living. Not a ghost or a statue: someone who eats, sleeps and walks to the market like everyone else. The difference is inside.
The text compares it to waking from a dream. In the dream there was a palace, a debt, a chase down a hallway. Nobody wakes up and pays the dream's debts.

That's how the free one holds the body's life, the book says: lightly, as something seen, not something that defines them. Then a qualifier: prarabdha holds only while someone takes themselves to be the body.
For the one who knows, it says, even that falls away. It's how many Hindus explain why even revered saints fell ill or grew old: the body's prarabdha plays out; the freedom never depended on it.
The one who knows lives an ordinary life, old arrows landing one by one, no new ones drawn. Some readers find that ending a relief. On this account, freedom isn't a life with no weather in it.
It means not mistaking the weather for yourself.

how: In Advaita Vedanta, teachers often explain the jivanmukta, the one free while living, through prarabdha karma: actions already begun play out in the body's life, while knowledge ends the mistaken sense of being bound by them.

o: knowing that stops new arrows, though old ones still land
a vow to stop all action so no karma is made
a store of facts about karma, learned from a teacher

games.q: the arrow and the dream — tap the pairs.
p: can't be called back by knowing

s: in the Vivekachudamani, the free person no longer has a body or ordinary needs
the free one still eats, sleeps and lives; actions already begun play out until they're spent.
the text compares actions already begun to an arrow already shot
the archer sees the tiger was a cow, but the arrow still lands where it was aimed.
on this account, knowing stops new arrows from being drawn
what knowing ends is the next reaction from the old mistake, not the arrows already flying.

games.q: you're the archer. the arrow is in the air, and you've just seen it's a cow. what happens?
o: the arrow lands where it was aimed.
games.why: knowing can't recall it. the text uses this to explain why a free person still lives out a body's life.

practice: Notice whatever the body is carrying right now, an ache, tiredness, a full stomach, a restless foot, and treat each one as an arrow already in flight: it will land, so let it.
Then watch the mind for the next arrow, the reaction that wants to be drawn, a complaint, a plan, a worry. Notice it, and leave the bow where it is.

wordCard.voice: Jnana. Knowing that frees: it can't call back the arrows already flying, but it stops drawing new ones.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: prarabdha, the karma that has already begun, the arrow already flying.
